content: 1. In 2015, Dooley et al. evaluated the safety and efficacy of dolutegravir-based antiretroviral therapy (ART) in adults co-infected with tuberculosis (TB) and HIV at week 24. This study was presented at the Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections (CROI) in Boston, MA, in 2018. 2. Manosuthi et al. conducted a randomized trial comparing plasma drug concentrations and efficacy between two non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)-based regimens in HIV-infected patients receiving rifampicin. This study, known as the N2R Study, was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in June 2009. 3. Mankhatitham et al. investigated hepatotoxicity in patients co-infected with TB and HIV-1 who were receiving NNRTI-based ART and rifampicin-containing anti-TB regimens. Their findings were published in the Southeast Asian Journal of Tropical Medicine and Public Health in 2011. 4. Sinha et al. conducted a pilot study in India comparing nevirapine-based and efavirenz-based ART regimens in antiretroviral-naïve patients with HIV and TB infections. The results were published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2013. 5. Sinha et al. also conducted a multi-center study in India comparing nevirapine-based and efavirenz-based ART regimens in antiretroviral-naïve patients with HIV and TB infections. This study was published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2017. 6. Swaminathan et al. performed a randomized clinical trial to assess the efficacy and safety of once-daily nevirapineor efavirenz-based ART in patients with HIV-associated TB. The results were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in October 2011. 7. Amogne et al. conducted the TB-HAART study, a randomized clinical trial evaluating the efficacy and safety of initiating ART one week after starting TB therapy in patients with CD4 counts below 200 cells/μL. The findings were published in PLoS ONE in 2015. 8. Kekitiinwa et al. studied the virologic response to first-line efavirenzor nevirapine-based ART in HIV-infected African children. Their findings were published in the Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal in June 2017. 9. Rudy et al. reported on immune reconstitution and persistent activation after 48 weeks of ART in youth with pre-therapy CD4 counts above 350. This study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2015. 10. Bienczak et al. identified that plasma efavirenz exposure, sex, and age predict virological response in HIV-infected African children. Their study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in October 2016. 11. Porter et al. reported a lack of emergent resistance in HIV-1-infected adolescents on elvitegravir-based single-tablet regimens. This was published in Topics in Antiviral Medicine in July 2015. 12. Gaur et al. evaluated the safety and efficacy of E/C/F/TAF in treatment-naïve HIV-1-infected adolescents. Their findings were published in Topics in Antiviral Medicine in June 2016. 13. Batra et al. presented week 24 data from a phase 3 clinical trial of E/C/F/TAF in HIV-positive adolescents. This study was published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society in April 2015. 14. Kizito et al. presented week 24 data from a phase 3 clinical trial of E/C/F/TAF in HIV-infected adolescents. Their findings were published in Topics in Antiviral Medicine in July 2015. 15. Shao et al. presented week 24 data from a phase 3 clinical trial of E/C/F/TAF in HIV-infected adolescents at the IAS Conference on HIV Science in 2015. 16. Pinto et al. conducted a phase II/III trial of lopinavir/ritonavir dosed according to WHO pediatric weight band dosing guidelines. Their findings were published in the Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal in February 2018. 17. The IMPAACT Network conducted a phase I/II multi-center, open-label study on the pharmacokinetics, safety, tolerability, and antiviral activity of dolutegravir in combination regimens for HIV-1-infected infants, children, and adolescents. 18. Amani-Bosse et al. studied virological response and resistance over 12 months in HIV-infected children under two years receiving first-line lopinavir/ritonavir-based ART in Côte d'Ivoire and Burkina Faso. This study was published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2017. 19. Pressiat et al. reported suboptimal cotrimoxazole prophylactic concentrations in HIV-infected children based on WHO guidelines. Their findings were published in the British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology in 2017. 20. Lombaard et al. evaluated the week 48 safety and efficacy of a rilpivirine-based regimen in treatment-naïve HIV-infected adolescents in the PAINT phase II trial. This study was published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2015. 21. Gopalan et al. reported sub-therapeutic nevirapine concentrations during ART initiation in HIV-infected children, highlighting implications for therapeutic drug monitoring. Their findings were published in PLoS ONE in August 2017. 22. Shiau et al. found that early initiation of ART in HIV-infected infants was associated with better virologic control after initial suppression. This study was published in AIDS in January 2017. 23. Jamieson et al. conducted a 48-week follow-up of the BAN randomized controlled trial, evaluating maternal and infant ART regimens to prevent postnatal HIV-1 transmission. Their findings were published in The Lancet in June 2012. 24. Gibb et al. studied pregnancy and infant outcomes among HIV-infected women on long-term ART with and without tenofovir in the DART trial. This study was published in PLoS Medicine in 2012. 25. Waitt et al. presented interim analysis from the DOLPHIN-1 study, comparing dolutegravir and efavirenz when initiating treatment in late pregnancy. This was presented at CROI in 2018. 26. Stek et al. investigated the pharmacokinetics of increased-dose darunavir during late pregnancy and postpartum. Their findings were published in Topics in Antiviral Medicine in June 2016. 27. Mulligan et al. studied dolutegravir pharmacokinetics in pregnant and postpartum women living with HIV. This study was published in AIDS in March 2018. 28. Lamorde et al. evaluated the pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and pharmacogenomics of efavirenz 400 mg once daily during pregnancy and postpartum. This was presented at the IAS Conference on HIV Science in 2017. 29. Shapiro et al. compared ART regimens in pregnancy and breastfeeding in Botswana. Their findings were published in the New England Journal of Medicine in June 2010. 30. Shapiro et al. also studied HIV transmission and 24-month survival in a randomized trial of HAART to prevent mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy and breastfeeding in Botswana. This study was published in AIDS in July 2013. 31. Ngoma et al. evaluated the efficacy of WHO recommendations for continued breastfeeding and maternal cART to prevent perinatal and postnatal HIV transmission in Zambia. Their findings were published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2015. 32. Fowler et al. assessed the benefits and risks of ART for perinatal HIV prevention. This study was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2016. 33. Fowler et al. also reported on the PROMISE trial, evaluating the efficacy and safety of two strategies to prevent perinatal HIV transmission. This was published in Topics in Antiviral Medicine in July 2015. 34. Cohan et al. compared the efficacy and safety of lopinavir/ritonavir versus efavirenz-based ART in HIV-infected pregnant Ugandan women. This study was published in AIDS in January 2015. 35. Koss et al. found that hair concentrations of antiretrovirals predicted viral suppression in HIV-infected pregnant and breastfeeding Ugandan women. This study was published in AIDS in April 2015. 36. Cohan et al. presented findings on the efficacy and safety of LPV/r versus EFV in HIV-positive pregnant and breastfeeding Ugandan women at CROI in 2014. 37. Koss et al. identified risk factors for preterm birth among HIV-infected pregnant Ugandan women randomized to lopinavir/ritonaviror efavirenz-based ART. This study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in October 2014. 38. Natureeba et al. compared lopinavir/ritonavir-based ART versus efavirenz-based ART for malaria prevention among HIV-infected pregnant women. This study was published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in December 2014. 39. Samuel et al. conducted a retrospective analysis of pregnancies exposed to antenatal atazanavir. Their findings were published in Infectious Diseases in Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2014. 40. Giuliano et al. found that high CMV IgG antibody levels were associated with a lower CD4+ response to ART in HIV-infected women. This study was published in the Journal of Clinical Virology in November 2017. 41. Palombi et al. reported on drug resistance mutations 18 months after discontinuation of nevirapine-based ART for prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV in Malawi. This study was published in the Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy in October 2015. 42. Andreotti et al. studied the impact of HBV or HCV co-infection in HIV-infected pregnant women receiving nevirapine-based ART in Malawi. This study was published in BMC Infectious Diseases in April 2014. 43. Palombi et al. evaluated antiretroviral prophylaxis for breastfeeding transmission in Malawi, focusing on drug concentrations, virological efficacy, and safety. This study was published in Antiviral Therapy in 2012. 44. Giuliano et al. assessed maternal ART for preventing mother-to-child transmission of HIV in Malawi, examining maternal and infant outcomes two years after delivery. This study was published in PLoS ONE in 2013. 45. Thorne et al. presented findings on pregnancy and neonatal outcomes following prenatal exposure to dolutegravir at the IAS Conference on HIV Science in 2017. 46. Bollen presented a comparison of dolutegravir pharmacokinetics during pregnancy and postpartum at the 18th International Workshop on Clinical Pharmacology of Antiviral Therapy in 2017. 47. Dooley et al. studied the pharmacokinetics of efavirenz and its use in treating HIV-1 among pregnant women with and without TB co-infection. This study was published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in January 2015. 48. Bussmann et al. reported pregnancy rates and birth outcomes among women on efavirenz-containing highly active ART in Botswana. This study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in July 2007. 49. Zash et al. compared the safety of dolutegravir and efavirenz initiated during pregnancy in Botswana. Their findings were published in The Lancet Global Health. 50. Zash et al. also reported that DTG/TDF/FTC initiated during pregnancy was as safe as EFV/TDF/FTC in nationwide birth outcomes surveillance in Botswana. This was presented at the IAS Conference on HIV Science in 2017.
